text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has agreed to pay the private contractor CSI Aviation up to $305.7m without competitive bidding on top of existing larger contracts and changed an existing agreement so that it can keep aircraft off public flight-tracking websites, federal contracting records show.
The change in September was to “add LADD”, the name of a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) program that prevents planes from appearing on some tracking websites. It may further inhibit monitoring of ICE flights, including flights to third countries, by immigrant and civil rights advocates.
On 31 October ICE also signed a new order with CSI worth up to $1.28bn to keep running its charter flights for another year in a deal that will also see CSI’s staff draw up the lists of people put on its deportation and transfer flights. Under ICE’s own handbook and the original terms of the agreement, supplying those lists was the agency’s job.
Neither the staffing deal, posted to a federal procurement website in July, nor the September contract change on flights have previously been reported in detail. The revelations show that despite protests and political reversals, the Trump administration’s ongoing deportation program is continuing to provide windfalls to private companies.
Angelina Godoy, director of the University of Washington’s Center for Human Rights, told the Guardian that she was “alarmed” by the contract, including the apparent intention to remove ICE flights from tracking websites.
“There is no legitimate reason to remove such flights from tracking systems; the only reason to do so is to seek further secrecy for the agency’s operations.” Godoy added, “It’s an affront to democracy and the rule of law for any government to be secretly shuttling people across the globe with no effective oversight or accountability for such operations.”
The Guardian contacted DHS, ICE and CSI Aviation for comment.
The staffing deal covers “up to 140 dedicated flight coordinators” at ICE field offices and air operations hubs, working “18 hours a day, 7 days a week”, according to a justification signed on 16 July by ICE’s head of contracting, Albert Dainton. The document says CSI is “the only source capable” of the work, citing its “proprietary systems” and “integrated flight tracking and manifest management systems that are interoperable with ICE’s operational platforms”. With options, the deal runs to March 2029, just after the scheduled end of Donald Trump’s term.
The justification says “increased operational demands now require these services”, and that “ICE field offices face challenges due to competing priorities and limited staffing”. The coordinators, it says, will “reduce administrative burdens on ICE personnel”.
These increased demands are apparently enough to induce DHS to disregard its own operational rules and to overturn the terms of previous contracts.
Under the original terms of the agreement, published by DHS in 2025, the government was to give CSI “a manifest containing the names of all passengers for each flight prior to departure”. ICE’s own air operations handbook assigns the work to agency staff. Its 2023 edition says ICE’s air removal coordinators are “responsible for reviewing and allocating seat requests, preparing flight manifests” in an agency system, the T-8 charter application.
CSI staff already had sweeping access to ICE data systems according to legal documents. In a sworn declaration filed in January in the US court of federal claims, where CSI unsuccessfully challenged a separate DHS contract, the company’s senior vice-president for government services, Richard DeLucia, said its personnel “have full access to ICE’s data systems to input data and verify manifests on every mission”. He said “the current program has evolved to capture more administrative functions for ICE ERO and to unburden ICE Officers so they can continue field operations”.
The same documents suggest a revolving door between the agencies and contractors. DeLucia said 19 of CSI’s more than 300 employees came from immigration agencies, “mostly recent retirees from ICE and CBP”, and that they handled “Immigration paperwork verification for all migrant domestic transfers and international removal missions”.
“We pride ourselves on hiring the best ICE personnel after they have left active duty to continue to bring a high level of continuity to our deportation system,” he wrote.
The September change adds LADD to the contract management section of the agreement, according to the federal award record. In aviation, LADD is the FAA’s Limiting Aircraft Data Displayed programme, under which aircraft owners and operators can keep their planes off public flight-tracking websites. The planes still broadcast their positions; the block changes what the websites display.
One flight-tracking site, FlightRadar24, reportedly received blocking notices under the programme for more than a dozen aircraft in March 2025, including planes often used for ICE deportations and transfers. The 2024 law behind the programme provides for blocking “upon request of a private aircraft owner or operator” for “the noncommercial flights of the owner or operator”. In May, 40 House Democrats wrote to the FAA citing “reports that ICE has misused” the programme “to shield deportation flights from public and congressional scrutiny”, and said that use was “out of the scope of this program”, the Guardian reported.
In an email, the New Jersey Democratic congressman Rob Menendez, one of the letter’s signatories, told the Guardian “ICE operates in near-secrecy, evading congressional oversight and making it almost impossible for families, their lawyers, and our casework teams to locate their loved ones.”
Menendez added that Democrats have “known for months that the Trump Administration has been abusing its ability to hide flights from public view. It was never intended to let ICE hide deportation flights from public scrutiny. That’s why we led over 30 of our colleagues in demanding answers from the FAA back in May, but the Administration continues to stonewall us.”
Menendez warned: “When Democrats take back the Majority next year, we will launch aggressive oversight into these secret flights and end ICE’s private flight secrecy once and for all.”
Fetaine Seddighzadeh of Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, one of the nonprofits that tracks ICE flights, told the Guardian in an email that “since late September, all ICE Air aircraft that previously showed visible tails became blocked on FlightAware and Flightradar24”, and that as of 5 November “the vast majority” of ICE flights could no longer be followed by their callsigns either. “With the absence of posted flight plans, we no longer know where removal and domestic shuffle flights are headed until the flight path is complete,” she said.
LADD binds commercial trackers such as Flightradar24 and FlightAware that use FAA data, but it “does nothing even against a casual observer, since many other aircraft trackers, including OpenSky or ADS-B Exchange, do not use FAA data and rely purely on crowdsourced ADS-B data which shows the aircraft”, said Martin Strohmeier, a board member of the OpenSky Network who researched aviation privacy at the University of Oxford. “Many charter aircraft operators put their aircraft on the list for one reason or another,” he said.
However, Seddighzadeh said that tracking the flights that way had become “an incredibly laborious process” at more than 70 ICE flights a day, and that the monitor’s work had “increased threefold since last year, reaching over 2,000 ICE flights per month”. Real-time tracking, she said, “may provide an early – and sometimes the only publicly visible – clue that a transfer or deportation is underway”.
“LADD blocks are the Trump administration’s latest attempt to further obscure its cruel deportation campaign,” Seddighzadeh said, calling it “this opaque and lawless system that has systematically violated due process, separated families, and uprooted thousands of people’s lives from communities across the country”.
The $1.28bn order was placed under a 2024 framework agreement that ICE awarded to CSI after receiving seven bids. However the staffing deal was not competitive, according to procurement records. Nor, reportedly, was a $562m order for flights that ICE placed with CSI in February 2025.
Rival bidders contested the framework agreement. In February 2025 one of them, Classic Air Charter, challenged CSI’s award at the US court of federal claims, after what its complaint called “five rounds of bid protest litigation”, arguing that ICE had evaluated CSI’s bid wrongly and allowed the company to “cure the defects in its quotation”. ICE staff then recommended terminating CSI’s award and cancelling the solicitation, a decision that government lawyers told the court belonged to the deputy homeland security secretary. ICE terminated the agreement in April 2025 “due to a protest at the Court of Federal Claims”, according to the federal award record.
In May ICE moved to reinstate it. Internal ICE emails released to the ACLU of Colorado after it sued under the Freedom of Information Act (Foia) show the request queued for approval at the top of DHS. “The ICE Air reinstatement was added back to the list as awaiting S2 approval (though I hear it’s actually S1 now for this one),” an ICE contract specialist wrote on 14 May 2025. S1 is DHS shorthand for the secretary, then Kristi Noem, whose office had to approve contracts worth more than $100,000.
A tracker of items awaiting the secretary’s approval still listed the reinstatement as “In Review” on 5 June. On 12 June ICE told the court it was “working to implement a proposal that would result in the voluntary dismissal” of the protest. Classic Air Charter dropped its challenge on 24 June. The federal record dates the reinstatement 25 June.
The Guardian contacted the ACLU of Colorado for comment.
Noem’s successor, Markwayne Mullin, rescinded the requirement for the secretary’s sign-off on contracts over $100,000 in April this year, as the Guardian previously reported. Dainton approved the staffing deal in both of the justification’s approval roles, as ICE’s advocate for competition and as its head of contracting.
The expanding relationship between DHS and CSI comes as the contractor faces a lawsuit over its role in flights that took Venezuelan men to a prison in El Salvador in March 2025. The Guardian reported on the commencement of that suit in July. The complaint, filed in Washington DC federal court, alleges CSI “remains the contractor responsible for brokering nearly all ICE Air flights for the Administration”.
On 12 November CSI asked the court to dismiss the case and to move it to Texas. In its filing, the company argued that “ICE (not CSI) had responsibility for the ‘manifest containing the names of all passengers for each flight’ (ie, identifying persons to be removed)”, citing the same contract clause.
In a sworn declaration filed alongside, CSI’s vice-president for government services, Andrew Talbott, said “ICE, not CSI, determined which individuals would board the planes”. CSI also argued that the complaint “does not allege that CSI was aware of the J.G.G. proceedings or that this Court’s orders were communicated to CSI”.
Godoy, the Center for Human Rights director, said ICE already had “considerable problems” with “putting people onto flights despite federal court orders having been issued prohibiting their transfer or deportation”.
“This would almost undoubtedly get worse if there were also private companies involved in the decisionmaking process, who would have to be notified by ICE of court rulings,” she said. Contractors, she added, “typically argue that Foia does not apply to them”.
digest_he:
רשות ההגירה והמכס של ארצות הברית הסכימה לשלם לחברה הפרטית CSI Aviation סכומים של עד מאות מיליוני דולרים ללא מכרז עבור הפעלת טיסות גירוש. במסגרת ההסכמים, שונתה מדיניות כך שטיסות הרשות הוסרו מאתרי מעקב פומביים באמצעות תוכנית ייעודית של רשות התעופה הפדרלית.

גורמים שונים ופעילים זכויות אדם הביעו ביקורת חריפה על המהלך, וטענו כי מדובר בניסיון להסתיר את פעילות הרשות מעין הציבור והפיקוח הקונגרסאונדי. מנגד, ברשות טוענים כי ההתקשרות נועדה להקל על העומס המנהלי ולאפשר פעילות שוטפת.
